hints: Focus on what the polymer backbone looks like after addition polymerisation, when the double bond opens to give two single-bonded chain carbons.
Draw but-2-ene as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$ and notice each double-bond carbon already has one H and one $\text{CH}_3$ group attached.
Join several of those monomers end to end and check that every new chain carbon still keeps its one H and one methyl, unlike monomers with a $\text{CH}_2$ end.
walkthrough:
**Picture what polymer Z needs**

Think of the long carbon backbone as a chain of -C-C-C-C- units. The question says every one of those backbone carbons carries one H and one $\text{CH}_3$ group.

So the repeat pattern must be:
$$-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-$$

**Recall how an alkene polymerises**

In addition polymerisation the C=C double bond opens up. Each of the two alkene carbons becomes a backbone carbon in the polymer and keeps the two groups it already had.

General rule:
$$n(\text{C=C}) \rightarrow -\text{C}-\text{C}-\text{C}-\text{C}-$$

**Test but-2-ene**

But-2-ene is $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH=CH}-\text{CH}_3$. Each C of the double bond is bonded to one H and one $\text{CH}_3$.

When many molecules join:
$$n\,\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3 \rightarrow -[\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)]_n-$$
This matches polymer Z exactly, so this is the monomer.

options.A: But-1-ene is $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. It polymerises to $-[\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3)]_n-$. One backbone carbon has two H atoms and the other has an ethyl group, not a methyl on every carbon.
options.B: But-2-ene is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$. Each alkene carbon has one H and one methyl. Opening the double bond gives $-[\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)]_n-$, so every chain carbon has exactly one H and one methyl as required.
options.C: Methylpropene is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CH}_2$. It polymerises to $-[\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2-\text{CH}_2]_n-$. This gives a carbon with two methyls and no H, and a carbon with two H atoms, the opposite of the description.
options.D: Propene is $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_3$. It polymerises to $-[\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)]_n-$. Only alternate carbons have a methyl group, while the $\text{CH}_2$ carbons have two H atoms, so not every carbon fits the rule.
